Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability mechanisms in web development, differentiating between stored and reflected XSS, and explains how un-sanitized user data (like query parameters or database entries) can execute malicious JavaScript on an origin, which is a fundamental platform security risk. modules: [SEC] topics: [platform security] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. platform security / Understanding the mechanics of Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), a code injection vulnerability where untrusted user data is combined with developer code and executed as JavaScript in the browser. Differentiating between Reflected XSS (where the malicious payload is delivered via the HTTP request, such as a crafted URL query parameter sent to a victim) and Stored XSS (where the payload is saved directly into the server's database, such as a MySpace profile, and executed automatically when any user views the page). The necessity of "escaping" HTML entities (e.g., converting < to <) so the browser treats the input as text rather than an executable script tag.

Look for. The definition of Reflected XSS: placing malicious code within an HTTP request (like a URL parameter) and tricking the user into clicking the link, which then executes the script in their browser. The definition of Stored XSS: inserting malicious code into the server database (e.g., via a profile update or HTTP header) so that the script runs automatically for anyone who visits the affected page. The specific method to neutralize XSS: "escaping" control characters (like <) into HTML entities (like <) so the browser renders them as plain text instead of executing them as code. The Samy MySpace worm example as a classic case of Stored XSS.
